text: Each actor in a story. <break time="0.8s" /> Should contribute in some way. <break time="0.8s" /> Sometimes characters are just fillers. <break time="0.8s" /> Can they be cut. <break time="0.8s" /> Or combined with another. <break time="0.8s" /> First time writers often have twins. <break time="0.8s" /> Or two brothers. <break time="0.8s" /> Who can be reduced to one. <break time="0.8s" /> With double the complexity. <break time="0.8s" /> By putting more than one function or role into a character. <break time="0.8s" /> It is possible. <break time="0.8s" /> To make them that much more interesting. <break time="0.8s" /> Each person should have some universally found quality. <break time="0.8s" /> That provides the reader with a shock of recognition. <break time="0.8s" /> Think Miss Havisham in Charles Dickenss Great Expectations. <break time="0.8s" /> Or Sethe, the tormented mother of Toni Morrisons Beloved. <break time="0.8s" /> But the most successful characters. <break time="0.8s" /> Should not be predictable. <break time="0.8s" /> And it can pay. <break time="0.8s" /> To have a person run. <break time="0.8s" /> Against the personality traits he or she has been given. <break time="0.8s" /> This is particularly true. <break time="0.8s" /> Of the most sympathetic, heroic creations. <break time="0.8s" /> They need that little drop of poison. <break time="0.8s" /> That the bee puts into honey to stop it going bad.
